summary.title: Reasons why SELECT * is bad for SQL performance
summary.one_liner: Selecting only the columns you need, instead of SELECT *, reduces network traffic, client and server CPU, sort/hash memory, and hard-parse cost, and can enable index-only scans and join elimination.
keywords: why not select star in production
takeaways: SELECT * sends more bytes over the network and costs more client-side CPU; the author's test with 3 of 16 columns ran over 2x faster (43s vs 95s).
Wide rows increase server-side sort and hash memory (232 MB vs 67 MB for a sort in one example) and CPU for datatype and character set conversion.
Naming only needed columns can allow index-only (index fast full) scans and Oracle join elimination, which SELECT * blocks.
Wide tables make hard parsing slower; a 1000-column SELECT * took about 78 ms of hard parse time in the author's test.
Explicit column lists also protect application code from breaking when columns are added or reordered.
summary.summary: The author lists reasons SELECT * hurts SQL performance when an application does not need every column, using Oracle examples measured with sqlplus, pSnapper, and Session Snapper. Each section compares a SELECT * query with a narrower column list and shows elapsed times, SQL*Net roundtrips, plan output, and memory use. Topics include network traffic, client and server CPU, optimizer transformations like index-only scans and join elimination, sort memory, and hard-parse overhead on wide tables. The article also mentions the sqlplus -fast and CSV options added in Oracle 12.2 for faster unloads.
